checkpoint.q: Rank the grading methods from cheapest to most expensive
checkpoint.a: Code-based grading (exact or string match) is cheapest, fastest and most reliable. LLM-based grading is next: scalable and flexible but it costs tokens and must be validated. Human grading is the most flexible and the most expensive and slowest, so the docs say to avoid it where possible and use it to calibrate the others.

checkpoint.q: Why must an LLM judge be validated, and against what?
checkpoint.a: A judge is itself a model whose scores can be consistent and still wrong, rewarding length, tone or its own biases instead of the criterion. Validate it against human-labelled examples of the same task and measure agreement before relying on it. Only then is the judge's score evidence about quality.

checkpoint.q: Which production signal reveals a silent regression that no error dashboard catches?
checkpoint.a: Quality signals on real traffic: online eval scores, user feedback such as thumbs-down or escalations, and shifts in output distributions such as category mix. A regression in answer quality returns HTTP 200, so error rates and latency stay green. Sampling production outputs back into the eval set closes the loop.
